This project aims to showcase my familiarity with testing APIs using Postman.

If you’re more interested in my ability to document APIs, please check out my downloadable project on electric vehicles—also available in my online portfolio.

Fundamental concepts

An extremely basic GET request

Let’s start with the most elementary thing possible: sending a simple API request. For this exercise, I will use an extremely lightweight API called "Cat Fact", which is primarily used to retrieve random cat facts using a GET request. Here’s a screenshot of the API:

To GET a random cat fact from this API in Postman, we’ll simply need to add the /fact endpoint to the its URL and paste it in the workspace while ensuring the "GET" method is selected.

https://catfact.ninja/fact

Note that the URL was pasted into the search bar. Once the request was sent, a random cat fact (e.g., the longest-living cat) appeared in the response section. The status displaying 200 OK indicates that the request worked as expected.

Storing and modifying URLs as variables

URLs can change without notice, and if a user has multiple requests using the same URL, a change would require them to update multiple URLs to ensure their requests work again. This can be a headache.

Therefore, it is generally best practice to save URLs as variables. If a URL changes, the user would only need to update the variable; the change would then be applied across all requests that use it.

Let’s save the URL of the request above as a variable.

As shown in the image above, the https://catfact.ninja URL has been saved as the Cat_URL variable.

When a URL is saved as a variable, any edits to it will automatically apply to every instance where it is used. This is by modifying the URL in the Current value field, which can be accessed in the collection edits.

A request with parameters

Usually, the goal of submitting a GET request is to obtain specific data. It is rare that we are satisfied with retrieving random data (as we did above) or returning a comprehensive list of all data items.

As such, many GET requests include parameters (and their values). These are used to narrow down our search so that more relevant data is returned. requests include parameters (and their values). These are used to narrow down our search so that more relevant data is returned.

In the example below, I’m querying the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration (NHTSA). By reviewing the API documentation, I learn that one of the endpoints allows me to get data on all car manufacturers. The parameters for this endpoint are:

  • 1) format: the format that I would like my data returned.

  • 2) page: the data that belongs on the specified page.

A GET request using this endpoint with the parameters above would look like this:

  • The endpoint is GetAllCarManufacturers

  • The format of the data to return is JSON

  • Only page 1 of the available data will be returned

As expected, the result is a list of car manufacturers—but in JSON format and limited to 100 entries, likely due to the first-page restriction.

A simple POST request

POST requests send data to a server or create or submit a new resource. Common uses of these requests include: submitting forms, adding new items in a database, posting content, uploading files, etc.

In our next example, let’s compose a POST request for a mock grocery store API.

According to the API documentation, I can use a POST request to create a new shopping cart using the /carts endpoint:

The body shows:

  • A new shopping cart created

  • A cart ID KhLRukfE1Ee-5ghb6uRS5 assigned

However, the newly created shopping cart is still empty. In the next section, we’ll try adding some items to it.

POSTing with JSON

Adding items to the newly created shopping cart requires a POST request /carts/:cartId/items with a body specifying the items we want. The items in the body must be written in JSON.

To begin, let’s start by writing the POST request. Note that the :cartId variable path here is simply a placeholder for the cart ID KhLRukfE1Ee-5ghb6uRS5 generated in the previous step.

Let’s say we want to add some coffee in the cart. By reviewing the documentation, we discover that its productId is 4646. This is sufficient information to allow us to create the body of our POST request:

As shown in the image above, two instances of item 4646 (i.e., coffee) has been added to the shopping cart, along with an item ID of 105522090. Tangentially, I also attempted to submit an array comprising of multiple items, but sadly this API doesn’t support that.

With a GET request with endpoint /carts/:cartId/items, we can even verify if our shopping cart now indeed contains two servings of coffee:

Modifying with PATCH

Upon POSTing our cart request, I realized that I actually wanted three, not two, cans of coffee. In order to modify the request, we can use the PATCH method to change an existing object’s properties.

The endpoint to modify cart items is /carts/:cartId/items/:itemId, where:

  • Our cart ID is KhLRukfE1Ee-5ghb6uRS5

  • Our item ID is 105522090

  • The quantity parameter is in the body and required

In Postman, the PATCH request should look like this:

The best practice here would be to save the cart and item IDs as variables, given that they have been used multiple times. This would prevent us from copying and pasting the values every time they are used

Upon submitting this PATCH request, the number of coffees in our cart should be updated. We can verify this by re-running a GET request with endpoint /carts/:cartId/items.

Replacing an item with PUT

Being the indecisive person that I am, I just realized that I want a different kind of coffee 4643. This means that I need to replace the previous coffee 4646 in my API request with this new coffee. This operation can be done using the PUT method, which can change an entire object rather than simply its properties.

The endpoint to replacing cart items is /carts/:cartId/items/:itemId, where:

  • Our cart ID is KhLRukfE1Ee-5ghb6uRS5

  • Our item ID is 105522090

  • The productId parameter is in the body and required

  • The quantity parameter is in the body and optional

Here’s the JSON body:

Submitting this PUT request should replace coffee 4646 with coffee 4643, which we can verify with a GET request.

DELETE-ing stuff

I just noticed that there was an unwanted product 8739in my shopping cart this whole time. I obviously don’t want to buy it. Thankfully, we can submit a DELETE request to remove it from the cart, using the endpoint /carts/:cartId/items/:itemId, where:

  • The cart ID is KhLRukfE1Ee-5ghb6uRS5

  • The item ID of the unwanted product is 15641062

After submitting the request, the GET request now shows our shopping cart without the unwanted product.

Built-in API tests

API tests help us quickly verify whether an API is functioning correctly. For instance, they can confirm if a response was sent successfully, how errors were managed, and even how long it took to receive a reply. While some of this information can be found by checking the console or backend, API tests provide a more efficient way to uncover these details.

For demonstration, let’s create a few API tests in JavaScript for the Weatherstack API. These tests will run each time we send the request they’re associated with.

  • The request: A GET request to retrieve the current temperature in Detroit, as shown below.

  • The API tests:

    • A test to confirm whether the API call was successful

    • A test to confirm whether the response time was less than 200ms

    • A test to confirm whether the response body includes the string Detroit

Luckily, Postman provides pre-written JavaScript code for simple requests like these. There’s no need for me to write them scratch; I can simply select them from Snippets and drop them into the post-response script text box, ensuring that these tests are run every time the request is executed.

Let’s test the API by running the request!

The results show that only two out of our three tests passed. The API call was successful, and the response body did include the string Detroit, but the response took longer than 200ms to return.

Here’s the body for reference:

By the way, the temperature in Detroit at the time the API request was sent was 3°F. Chilly!

Writing our own test

Obviously, it is possible that we’ll need to write our own test(s). After all, the available snippets in Postman can be quite limited.

One crucial test we should include is checking whether the response body actually contains a temperature — specifically, a numeric value. It would be problematic if that weren’t the case.

Here’s the annotated test I wrote, along with proof that it passed:

If we go over to the response body, we can confirm that the temperature is indeed a number.

Detroit is my favorite city, so it deserves to be stored as a variable in a Postman collection. As mentioned before, variables make writing API requests a more efficient process, especially when it involves jotting down multiple numbers or letters, such as API keys, tokens, or ID numbers. Excluding tests based on different environments

In the real world, it is customary for developers, programmers, and indeed API testers, to work in different environments. For example, a developer fixing a bug may push their change from the testing environment to the staging environment.

This concept can be replicated in Postman, as it allows us to create multiple environments.

In the weather API example, I created two separate environments: Testing and Production.

As shown in the image above, the tests associated with the GET temperature request have been automatically migrated to the Production environment upon its creation. However, it makes sense to exclude these tests in this environment, as they should belong to the Testing environment. Querying the API in the Production environment should only result in temperature data.

Thankfully, it is possible to write some code to exclude test blocks. See the image below:

This simple If statement ensures that the test block it encompasses will only run if the Postman environment is equal to Testing. If we now run the Production environment, these tests should not be run.

As shown in the image above, the test results section is empty.

The Spotify API collection

We now know enough to start creating our first "real" API collection. For the purpose of this project, we will use Spotify, which allows us to query a bunch of fun information about songs, artists, as well as my personal user data.

Our plan is to start by building a series of API requests and run some manual tests.

Getting access to the API

Like any self-respecting API, the Spotify API requires the user to gain an access token in order to start using it.

Spotify’s official documentation covers the process in cURL. However, because we are using Postman, the process is significantly more intuitive.

The first step in obtaining an access token is to create a Spotify Developer Account, which is required to generate a client ID and client secret.

Once that’s done, I store my client ID and client secret as variables in a newly created Spotify environment.

This in turn allows me to fill up the authorization request headers in Postman:

Most of these fields have been completed based on the instructions in the Spotify documentation, but do note:

  • Client ID and client secret are entered as environment variables.

  • The scope defines the types of endpoints we can access. In our case, it shall be restricted to reading data rather than creating or modifying it.

Once the authorization request headers have been filled correctly, I can request a new access token. See the received access token:

I should now have all I need to start creating API requests in my Spotify collection.

GET new releases

One of the most basic requests we can make with the Spotify API is to get a list of the newest releases. The endpoint is as follows:

  • v1/browse/new-releases

With the following parameters:

  • limit: Determines the number of results returned

  • offset: Determines the index of the first result returned

Sadly, Spotify doesn’t tell us the logic behind its indexing.

Our request looks like this in Postman:

Where:

  • Only two results will be returned

  • The first two indexed results will be returned

The response body is a bit long to fit in a single screenshot, but the two releases returned are albums from Charli XCX and Jelly Roll, respectively.

GET artist’s top tracks

Another simple request we can make with the Spotify API is to retrieve a given artist’s top tracks, with their Spotify ID as a path variable identifier. The endpoint is as follows:

  • v1/artists/:id/top-tracks: Where :id/ is the artist’s Spotify ID to be used as a path variable.

For the purpose of this exercise, we will be looking up data on one of my favorite artists: Krayzie Bone. His Spotify ID is 53B8dEQzmtefvkdCAkO0YR. In Postman, the API request looks like this:

Again, the response body is way too long to be copied here, as it retrieves the data on all of Krayzie Bone’s best tracks.

However, based on my Spotify App, his most popular track by monthly listens is called…​I don’t Give a Fuck. Therefore, we should expect this track to be within the response body. In fact, it should even be the first track to be returned, given as it is the most popular of the bunch.

The following API tests confirm just that:

GET my saved tracks

The very cool v1/me/tracks endpoint allows the user to retrieve their very own saved tracks on their account. Let’s try it out!

Where:

  • Only the 10 most recent saved tracks will be retrieved, as limit = 10

Here’s the response body, which shows us a glimpse of my most recent favorite tracks.

Now, let’s write some tests to make sure the API responded correctly. First, I would like to make sure that a recent addiction of mine called Hooked is part of the response body. Second, I want to make sure that there were actually 10 items returned.

POST a playlist

Most people probably use the Spotify API to create playlists, so we’ll do the same here. According to official documentation, the endpoint for this POST method is as follows:

  • v1/users/:user_id/playlist: Where :user_id/ is my personal user ID.

The first step, of course, is to find my user ID and save it as a variable in the environment.

Once that is done, we’ll need to write a request body in JSON, as all POST methods require. For this endpoint, the request body uses the following format:

{
    "name": "New Playlist",
    "description": "New playlist description",
    "public": false
}

Here is the request body in Postman:

After submitting the request, we receive a response confirming that a blank playlist has been successfully created under my name.

As for the API test associated with this request, we can simply include a status code check:

Finally, let’s look ahead a bit: the next logical step is to add songs to this playlist, and I suspect the endpoint will require the playlist ID. Instead of manually copying and pasting the playlist ID into the request body every time, we can write a test to automatically save the ID as a variable whenever the request is executed. This way, we can use this variable in the subsequent endpoint and always ensure the correct playlist ID is included automatically.

POSTing songs to the playlist

Now that we have a working playlist, we can add a song to it. For the purpose of this demonstration, I will only add one song: Hip-Hop Baby by Layzie Bone. The endpoint for POSTing is as follows:

  • v1/playlists/:playlist_id/tracks

With the following query parameters and path variables:

  • uris: The query parameter to select the song to add, where the value is spotify:track:26qTSERT9SkyHXhfgSTiGMfor the song Hip-Hop Baby.

  • playlist_id: The path variable to select the playlist to add to. In our case, we are using an environment variable that represents the ID of the previously created playlist. A test was implemented to ensure that the variable will always use the latest playlist created.

Upon sending the request, the response body generates a snapshot ID, which we can confirm with a test:

For what is worth, we can even go on my Spotify and verify that the playlist and song were created.

DELETE-ing the playlist

Lastly, to ensure that I won’t clutter my Spotify account with demo playlists every time I run these requests, I will finish up a DELETE request. That way, I won’t need to manually delete these mock playlists in my actual Spotify account whenever I’m done running these requests on Postman.

The endpoint to delete a playlist is as follows:

  • v1/playlists/:playlist_id/followers

With the following query parameter:

  • playlist_id: Which follows the logic elaborated above.

Running this request should delete the playlist associated with the ID above. A test can be included to confirm that the playlist has indeed been deleted.

Running tests

In the previous section, we created a list of requests that interact with the Spotify API. Additionally, we designed multiple tests for each request and ran them to verify the requests work as intended. However, the process of running tests for each request can be time-consuming, especially if the collection includes a large number of requests.

Thankfully, Postman offers a "collection runner" feature that allows the user to quickly and sequentially run all tests for each request within a collection. In the image below, I accessed the runner through my Spotify collection—notice how the requests are arranged in order and how there is a button to run the entire collection at once.

Postman spent exactly 1.381 seconds to run all my tests, displaying that they have all passed.

To be continued…​

It is painfully clear that the elephant in the room here is the lack of automated testing via tools such as Postman CLI, Newman, or Jenkins. Sadly, learning these tools is currently not within my bandwidth, though it is certainly on my radar.

I actually started experimenting with these tools but ran into several roadblocks that I could not easily troubleshoot. It is therefore with great regret that I have to set this endeavor aside for now and plan to revisit it at a later date.
